title: Heather Page
tagline: How a chief of staff's work shows up in public: an operator's role, a host's microphone, and a writing voice that moved from bank-modernization frameworks to weekly AI commentary.
credit: An independent StoryTellr study by Nikhil Khedkar.
disclaimer: Built only from Heather Page's public professional work (TribalScale pages, a company-published interview, podcast listings, and the TribalScale Substack), read on 2026-09-30. Nothing about her private life is included. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Heather Page or TribalScale; most sources are published by TribalScale.

nodes.title: Heather Page
nodes.summary: Chief of Staff at TribalScale, a technology consultancy with offices in Toronto, New York and Miami; in public she is an operator, a podcast host, and a bylined writer.
nodes.evidence: Heather Page is the Chief of Staff at TribalScale.

nodes.title: Chief of Staff
nodes.summary: The job was created when the CEO went looking for a Chief of Staff in late 2020; it is the thread that runs through everything else she publishes.
nodes.details: The 2022 interview is a company-published piece, so it tells TribalScale's version of how the role was set up. It says the job focused on operations accountability, following up on plans and goals, relationship management, and strategic partnerships.
nodes.evidence: our CEO Sheetal Jaitly began searching for a Chief of Staff to add to his team.

nodes.title: CEO's sounding board
nodes.summary: Her own short definition of the job: a safe place for the CEO to test half-formed ideas.
nodes.evidence: a sounding board for the CEO to bounce ideas off of without judgement

nodes.title: The 30-60-90 day plan
nodes.summary: The role began as a written plan: she and the CEO built the job description and a 90-day plan together, after she spoke with other leaders.
nodes.evidence: including the development of a 30–60–90 day plan to overcome the obstacles that TribalScale was facing

nodes.title: A Chief of Staff with no COO
nodes.summary: Because TribalScale had no COO, the role was more hands-on with operations than the moonshot-and-partnerships version of the job.
nodes.evidence: because we don’t have a COO, Heather is able to keep most of those COO responsibilities within the CEO’s office

nodes.title: Regular team check-ins
nodes.summary: Her method for seeing how the company really works: ongoing check-ins across the whole team, with insights passed to the CEO.
nodes.evidence: implementing regular check-ins to understand how people work and what is not working for them

nodes.title: Shaping senior hiring
nodes.summary: She was involved in senior hires from her first days and helped shape the hiring process.
nodes.evidence: playing a key role in hiring senior staff members since day one

nodes.title: Working with the leadership team
nodes.summary: The interview names the colleagues she worked most closely with across revenue, product/design, and engineering.
nodes.details: Titles as of March 2022: Chief Revenue Officer Rich Gigante, VP of Product/Design Krys Krycinski, Director of Engineering Jason Mills.
nodes.evidence: regularly communicates with our senior leaders including our Chief Revenue Officer, Rich Gigante

nodes.title: MBA and a decade in tech
nodes.summary: The only professional background the sources give: an MBA and roughly ten years across customer success, marketplace management, and chief-of-staff roles.
nodes.details: Employers before TribalScale are not named in any source read for this study, so none are listed.
nodes.evidence: an MBA from the Schulich School of Business, and has close to 10 years of experience in the tech industry

nodes.title: First Name Basis podcast
nodes.summary: TribalScale's podcast; in 2022 she hosted two guest conversations and was herself interviewed once.
nodes.evidence: Apple Podcasts dates the four episodes involving her 2022-05-12, 2022-05-19, 2022-06-23 and 2022-11-03.

nodes.title: Workplace wellness series
nodes.summary: A two-part conversation she hosted for Mental Health Awareness Month with the co-founder of Inward Strong; the subject is the guest's field, not the host's.
nodes.evidence: For Mental Health Awareness Month, Host Heather Page is joined by Monique Peats, Co-founder and Chief Clinical Director at Inward Strong.

nodes.title: Episode: The Chief of Staff Role
nodes.summary: The episode where the roles flip: the CEO interviews her about the job, her work with the leadership team, and challenges she overcame.
nodes.details: Only the episode description was read, not the audio.
nodes.evidence: This week TribalScale CEO, Sheetal Jaitly, is joined by our Chief of Staff, Heather Page.

nodes.title: Episode: Gender Equity in Web3
nodes.summary: She hosted the founder of Web3 Equity on skill-building for allies, accessibility challenges, and the Web3 community in Miami.
nodes.evidence: TribalScale Chief of Staff, Heather Page, is joined by Michelle Abbs, Founder and CEO of Web3 Equity

nodes.title: Modernization Index
nodes.summary: The scoring framework behind her financial-services series: four pillars scored on a scale where 3 means 'standardizing' and 5 means 'adaptive'.
nodes.evidence: Data Foundation & Architecture, Governance & Regulatory Readiness, AI & Real-Time Decisioning, and Customer Intelligence & Personalization

nodes.title: The six profiles (and hybrids)
nodes.summary: The capstone of a six-part series: six archetypes of a bank's modernization, with the argument that real institutions are hybrids that migrate over time.
nodes.details: Only two of the six profile articles appear on her profile page's visible list; the byline of the other four was not checked.
nodes.evidence: The six archetypes are models, not identities.

nodes.title: The AI Experimenter
nodes.summary: Profile 1 of 6: strong AI pilots sitting on a weak data and governance base, which keeps the pilots from scaling.
nodes.details: Its recommended move is to freeze the model inventory and spend two quarters on data foundation and governance. The article calls it the most common profile in financial services; that is TribalScale's claim.
nodes.evidence: AI & Real-Time Decisioning scores a 3.5 or higher.

nodes.title: The Balanced Modernizer
nodes.summary: The contrarian profile: an institution with no weak pillar, which she argues is stuck because nothing forces a concentrated bet.
nodes.evidence: Data Foundation is at 3.2. Governance is at 3.5. AI & Real-Time Decisioning is at 3.0. Customer Intelligence is at 3.3.

nodes.title: Beyond Inheritance
nodes.summary: A warning to banks that heirs who receive boomer wealth may not keep the accounts their parents held.
nodes.details: The figures are stated in the article without citation. The rest of the piece is in the gated FinScale magazine download and was not read.
nodes.evidence: $84 trillion moving from baby boomers to their heirs over the next two decades

nodes.title: The Nostalgia Gold Mine
nodes.summary: Off-topic for banking: media companies' content archives as an asset, using Disney+ and Formula 1 as examples.
nodes.evidence: Think of it like a museum curator rather than a warehouse manager.

nodes.title: Call Centers: The Untapped Goldmine
nodes.summary: Her piece in FinScale Vol. 2, listed by title and byline only; the article itself sits inside the magazine download and was not read.
nodes.evidence: Call Centers: The Untapped Goldmine (by Heather Page)

nodes.title: FinScale magazine
nodes.summary: TribalScale's digital magazine for banking and insurance leaders, which carries at least two of her pieces.
nodes.evidence: a new digital publication dedicated to providing insights and strategies for the financial services and insurance (FSI) industries

nodes.title: A Brief History of Toronto's Tech Events
nodes.summary: Her community-history essay: Toronto's tech scene was built event by event by practitioners, and institutions followed.
nodes.evidence: In 2017, we rented out the Arcadian Court, booked 30 speakers from six countries, and called it TakeOver.

nodes.title: Xtreme Labs lineage
nodes.summary: The Toronto product studio whose alumni, including TribalScale's CEO, carried its culture into the wider scene.
nodes.details: The essay says the CEO was Director of Business Development at Xtreme and later moved into telecommunications and IoT under Pivotal, which acquired Xtreme.
nodes.evidence: Founded in 2007 by Amar Varma and Sunny Madra

nodes.title: TakeOver conference
nodes.summary: TribalScale's own contribution to the scene: a Toronto innovation conference run in 2017 and 2018.
nodes.details: The essay is inconsistent about the first year: one paragraph says it brought together 600 executives, investors and leaders, another says over 800 attended. Both figures are the company's; neither is resolved here. For 2018 it reports a sell-out with 1,700 attendees and the debut of the Venture Studios program.
nodes.evidence: We did our first TakeOver in 2017 with over 800 attendees.

nodes.title: From grassroots to government
nodes.summary: The essay's argument: public institutions arrived after the community had already shown what it could do, from FITC and MaRS to Collision.
nodes.evidence: from passive to participatory, after the community put in the work

nodes.title: Toronto Tech Week
nodes.summary: The essay's endpoint and its timing hook: a city-backed, multi-year grassroots tech week.
nodes.evidence: The 2025 debut brought together more than 15,000 attendees across 315 events and 500 speakers spanning 27 neighbourhoods

nodes.title: TribalScale Substack
nodes.summary: A company newsletter launched in late 2025 that now carries her byline on nearly every post; it is where her public writing shifted to AI strategy.
nodes.details: The archive lists 23 posts from 2025-10-30 to 2026-09-30; 22 show Heather Page in the byline field. How each post was drafted is not stated, so this study says 'bylined', not more. Several posts are curated commentary with reading lists.
nodes.evidence: We’ve launched our Substack as a home for deeper thinking on technology, transformation, and the future of how we build.

nodes.title: 88% use it, 7% scaled it
nodes.summary: Her diagnosis of enterprise AI: the gap is organizational, not technical, because no one tied the pilot to a business outcome.
nodes.details: The figures come from a McKinsey survey as reported in the essay; she also cites a Publicis Sapient survey.
nodes.evidence: Only 7% of companies say they’ve fully scaled AI across their organization.

nodes.title: The 'could you explain it' test
nodes.summary: TribalScale's stated internal gate for shipping an agent feature, offered in the essay as the practice that separates products from demos.
nodes.details: This is a company statement about its own process, not independently verified.
nodes.evidence: could you explain why it just did that? If you can’t, you don’t have a product, you have a demo.

nodes.title: Where AI lock-in really lives
nodes.summary: Her argument that vendor lock-in sits in workflows, memory and institutional context rather than in the model API.
nodes.details: The essay reports that 58% of those who tried to switch said the migration failed or cost far more than expected. A related essay asks, of OpenAI's new deployment company, 'embedded by whom, and building toward what?'
nodes.evidence: 90% of executives believed they could switch AI vendors within four weeks.

nodes.title: Flagging who is selling
nodes.summary: A recurring move in her posts: noting when a cited survey or figure comes from a party with something to sell.
nodes.details: Three examples across posts: Publicis Sapient (org-redesign work), Zapier (workflow orchestration), DXC's own delivery estimates.
nodes.evidence: Worth noting those figures are DXC’s own estimates, not independently verified.

nodes.title: The case for building cheap
nodes.summary: A report on TribalScale's own internal agents, used to argue that simple, governed architectures beat expensive ones in early adoption.
nodes.details: All figures, including the four-month timeline and the days-to-15-minutes case-study claim, are TribalScale's own and unverified.
nodes.evidence: The platform runs for $20-40 USD per day across all active workflows.

nodes.title: Daily cycles, not sprints
nodes.summary: Her opinion that if AI collapses the cost of drafting code, the two-week sprint is sized for a bottleneck that has shrunk.
nodes.evidence: teams should move to daily cycles, not two-week ones.

nodes.title: Proximity beats documentation
nodes.summary: A rare post where she writes about TribalScale's origins: builders in the room with the people they build for are the structural answer to misalignment, more so when agents multiply it.
nodes.evidence: proximity is the only structural answer to the alignment problem

nodes.title: TribalScale
nodes.summary: The technology consultancy that employs her and publishes nearly everything in this study.
nodes.evidence: Our method blends human-centred design, agile cycles, and AI-powered engineering.

nodes.title: Sheetal Jaitly
nodes.summary: TribalScale's CEO: the person she works for, interviews on the podcast, and whose background she traces in her origins post.
nodes.details: Identified in the sources as the CEO who founded TribalScale in November 2015 after Xtreme Labs and Pivotal.
nodes.evidence: Sheetal Jaitly, CEO of TribalScale

nodes.title: How TribalScale works
nodes.summary: The company's stated method: five steps from Frame to Next Bets, worked in tight cycles.
nodes.evidence: We work in tight cycles—aligning daily, shipping weekly, pivoting instantly.

nodes.title: Design writing: not found
nodes.summary: An honest gap: no design-process or AI-design-process writing under her name turned up; the closest thread is her profile's line about customer pain points.
nodes.details: Her profile page shows a 'Load More' after six articles, and the full list could not be expanded. The Substack archive titles contain no design-process post by her; one design-led piece summarises a FinScale article by Anna Foat.
nodes.evidence: creating solutions that solve meaningful pain points

stories.title: The operator
stories.summary: What the job is, in her and the company's words: a role built around listening to the whole team and translating it for the CEO.

stories.title: Built event by event
stories.summary: Her one history essay is also the company's origin story: Toronto's scene, the studio that seeded its founder, and the conference TribalScale ran itself.

stories.title: Naming the stuck bank
stories.summary: A scoring framework turned into a cast of archetypes, each with a recommended move; the point is a shared vocabulary for where an institution is.

stories.title: Why AI stalls, according to the newsletter
stories.summary: Across posts the claim holds together: pilots stall on organization and unclear definitions of working, lock-in lives in workflows, and the writer keeps noting who benefits from each statistic.

stories.title: What the page does not show
stories.summary: The requested design-process thread is missing from her public writing; this path marks where it would sit and what the nearest material is.
